front: Mon char est stationné en face.
back: My car is parked across the street.
context: Québec: 'un char' = a car (France: une voiture). 'Stationner' = to park (France: se garer).

front: Je vais magasiner au centre d'achats.
back: I'm going shopping at the mall.
context: 'Magasiner' = to shop (France: faire du shopping). 'Un centre d'achats' = a mall.
'Plate' = boring. 'Ben' = bien (really).
'Tiguidou' = great, all good. Very Québécois.
In Québec 'bienvenue' also means 'you're welcome', a calque of English.
'Frette' = very cold. 'À matin' = ce matin.

back: Put your winter hat on, it's snowing.
context: 'Une tuque' = a knitted winter hat (France: un bonnet).
'Être tanné' = to be fed up.

front: J'ai de la misère à comprendre son accent.
pronunciation: [zhay duh lah mee-ZEHR ah kohm-prahn-druh soh nak-SAHN]
back: I have trouble understanding his accent.
context: 'Avoir de la misère à' = to have difficulty (France: avoir du mal à).

front: Ma blonde pis moi, on part en fin de semaine.
pronunciation: [mah BLOHND pee MWAH, ohn par ahn fan duh suh-MEN]
back: My girlfriend and I are going away this weekend.
context: 'Ma blonde' = my girlfriend (whatever her hair color). 'Pis' = and/then. 'La fin de semaine' = the weekend.

front: C'est mon chum depuis le cégep.
back: He's been my boyfriend since college.
context: 'Un chum' = boyfriend or buddy. 'Le cégep' = pre-university college.

front: Je vais au dépanneur chercher du lait.
pronunciation: [zhuh veh zoh day-pah-NUHR shehr-shay dü LEH]
back: I'm going to the corner store for some milk.
context: 'Le dépanneur' (le dep) = convenience store.

front: On déjeune à sept heures, on dîne à midi pis on soupe à six heures.
pronunciation: [ohn day-zhuhn ah set UHR, ohn deen ah mee-DEE pee ohn soop ah see ZUHR]
back: We have breakfast at seven, lunch at noon and dinner at six.
context: Québec keeps the old meal names: déjeuner, dîner, souper.
The particle '-tu' turns a statement into a yes/no question, even with 'tu': 'tu veux-tu un café ?'

back: I'm freaking out, it's so beautiful!
context: 'Capoter' = to go crazy (with joy or panic).
'Niaiser' = to joke around, or to waste someone's time.
'Le fun' (pronounced 'fonne') = fun. 'En masse' = a lot.
'Être en beau fusil' = to be hopping mad.
'Ça a pas d'allure' = that makes no sense. Note the dropped 'ne', typical of informal speech.
Astonishment or exasperation, nothing to do with travel.
'Achaler' = to annoy.

front: Elles ont placoté toute la soirée.
context: 'Placoter' = to chat, gossip.

front: J'avais la chienne avant mon examen.
back: I was scared stiff before my exam.
context: 'Avoir la chienne' = to be scared (informal).

front: On va prendre une marche après souper.
pronunciation: [ohn vah prahn-druh ün MARSH ah-preh soo-PAY]
back: We'll go for a walk after dinner.
context: Calque of English 'take a walk' (France: faire une promenade).
'Une piastre' (piasse) = a dollar, informal.
'Faque' (fait que) = so, a very frequent spoken connector.
'Courriel' was coined in Québec and recommended in France too, where 'un mail' still dominates.

front: Au Québec, les panneaux disent « Arrêt » et non « Stop ».
pronunciation: [oh kay-BEK, lay pah-NOH deez ah-REH ay nohn STOP]
context: A visible sign of Québec's language policy.

front: La loi 101 a fait du français la seule langue officielle du Québec.
pronunciation: [lah lwah sahn-AN ah feh dü frahn-SEH lah suhl lahng oh-fee-SYEL dü kay-BEK]
back: Bill 101 made French the sole official language of Québec.
context: The Charter of the French Language, 1977.
De Gaulle's 1967 cry from Montréal city hall caused a diplomatic crisis with Canada.
Fries, cheese curds and gravy. Note the Québec 't' → 'ts' before i.

back: Are you saying that as a joke?
context: Accent: 't' and 'd' before i and u become 'ts' and 'dz': 'tsu dzis'.
'Icitte' = ici, from old French. Many Québec words preserve 17th-century usage.
In Québec 'bonne fête' = happy birthday; France says 'joyeux anniversaire'.
Québec's motto, printed on every licence plate.
